subjects.displayTitle: Tests and trials; sacrifice and suffering
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh teaches that God has always tried His servants so that light can be told from darkness and roses from thorns, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá likens the soul to ground that yields a richer harvest the more deeply it is ploughed. Trial, then, is no verdict on the one who suffers. The storm does not rise to sink the ship but follows its own course, and a sturdy vessel rides it out; immolation in the days of Abraham meant a station of sacrifice, freedom from desire, not the shedding of blood. Yet the same teachings refuse to turn pain into a formula: affliction is not proof of sin, grief and fatigue are real, and the sick and the bereaved need practical care rather than explanation. Trust walks beside prudence, forgiveness beside appeals for justice, endurance beside the quiet work of planting a garden while a city is in turmoil. From here the path opens toward the mystery of sacrifice and the hard questions of theodicy, and toward the gentler disciplines of consolation, detachment and steadfastness, where what was endured becomes something offered.

shortened: Abdu'l-Baha. -- 'The mind and spirit of man advance when he is tried by suffering. The more the ground is ploughed the better the seed will grow, the better the harvest will be. Just as the plough furrows the earth deeply, purifying it of weeds and thistles, so suffering and tribulation free man from the petty affairs of this worldly life until he arrives at a state of complete detachment. His attitude in this world will be that of divine happiness. Man is, so to speak, unripe: the heat of the fire of suffering will mature him. Look back to the times past and you will find that the greatest men have suffered most.'

This passage is from a letter written on behalf of Shoghi Effendi on 6 October 1954, reproduced in Living the Life, extract 68, inside a later 2021 letter. Its context connects study, spiritual growth and sustained service. The original attribution remains 1954.
shortened: Naturally there will be periods of distress and difficulty, and even severe tests; but if that person turns firmly toward the divine Manifestation, studies carefully His spiritual teachings and receives the blessings of the Holy Spirit, he will find that in reality these tests and difficulties have been the gifts of God to enable him to grow and develop. Thus you might look upon your own difficulties in the path of service. They are the means of your spirit growing and developing.

shortened: As long as there will be life on earth, there will also be suffering, in various forms and degrees. But suffering, although an inescapable reality, can nevertheless be utilized as a means for the attainment of happiness. This is the interpretation given to it by all the Prophets and saints, who, in the midst of severe tests and trials, felt happy and joyous and experienced what is best and holiest in life. Suffering is both a reminder and a guide.

questions: What meanings do these readings give to trial, sacrifice, consequence and temptation? Compare the complete questions and answers, James 1:2–18, and the neighbors on theodicy and the mystery of sacrifice. Where does each explanation acknowledge limits?

How do historical accounts of persecution and exile connect individual endurance with a wider purpose? What changes when journeys, prayers and narratives are read in full? Explore suffering and imprisonment and the sacrifice of the Manifestation, preserving distinctions between testimony, reported speech and translation.

What do wealth, praise, influence, expectation and fear disclose about character? How do the passages on courage, humility, forgiveness and renewed effort complicate a simple division between strong and weak people? What would honest self-examination involve?

How can hope and patience coexist with grief, fatigue, illness and uncertainty? Compare the letters to bereaved people, the complete prayers and Job 42:7–9. What makes consolation attentive to another person’s experience and practical needs?

How do trust, prudence, justice and protection work together? Compare refusals to test God through danger, protective travel decisions, appeals for justice and wishes for relief. What distinguishes nonretaliation from allowing avoidable harm to continue?

What forms can sacrifice take in daily service and mutual assistance? Explore the neighbors on sacrifice of self, steadfastness and spiritual struggle. How might a family or community share burdens, respect capacity and turn reflection into a concrete act of care?
